## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.00425.015](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.00425.015)

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for choosing to send your work entitled “Decoding the neural mechanisms of human tool use” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been evaluated by a Senior editor and 3 reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The following individuals responsible for the peer review of your submission want to reveal their identity: Dora Angelaki (Reviewing editor) and Brad Mahon (peer reviewer).

The Reviewing editor and the other reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

The paper is clearly written and organized, and tackles an important question with a well-thought-out and sophisticated approach. Overall this is excellent work, although there are some concerns/questions that the authors should address:

1) An aspect of the Results that is not sufficiently brought out up front in the article (Abstract and Introduction) is that in different regions it is possible to distinguish different factors within the experiment. For instance, the fact that in pMTG upcoming actions can be decoded only when they are performed with the tools, whereas in Superior parietal-occipital cortex decoding was higher for the hand than for the tool, is a really important aspect of the findings that is somewhat buried. The authors should bring this out more fully.

2) It seems somewhat surprising that the regions able to decode across effector (tool→hand, hand→tool) are in IPS and premotor cortex, while regions within IPS/premotor cortex were also shown to have better decoding for hand than for tools. How can the authors reconcile these different effects (are they different populations of voxels driving the decoding accuracy?). Perhaps plotting the weights, voxel-wise, could help to address this.

3) It would be good to see the results (e.g., in figure form, and reduced statistics) for the control analysis of decoding of the ventricle and outside of the brain. This analysis addresses a really insidious issue that will be at the forefront of skeptical readers’ minds; it should be dealt with in full (rather than just saying the analysis was performed and there were no effects).

4) In discussing the occipital-temporal decoding of upcoming actions, the authors come close to, but shy away from, considering whether the organization of the ventral stream may be constrained by the way that the ventral stream is connected up with the rest of the brain (e.g., specificity for the visual representations of body parts could be driven by connectivity to regions of somatosensory or motor areas, and the same for regions that represent tools). The authors’ findings, showing that occipital temporal regions can decode upcoming actions would seem to resonate with that type of an explanation of the causes of neural specificity for different classes of visual stimuli in the ventral stream, at least as it applies to the representation of tools.

5) The auditory cue to determine the subjects’ movement seems to have been the same for both the hand and tool conditions. This consistency across effectors could be responsible for some or even all of the apparently cross-effector classification. That is, the activity in the ROIs that show above-chance cross-effector decoding of actions could be due to the content of the cue rather than preparation for the action per se. This issue must be addressed.

6) It was not clear that the authors balanced the number of voxels across ROIs. This is potentially important as other studies have shown that MVPA performance is strongly influenced by the number of voxels tested.

7) The authors averaged across both directions of the cross-effector test (hand→tool and tool→hand). It is possible however that there are asymmetries in action coding that would be revealed by disentangling these tests.

8) While the authors find that the univariate response properties of regions generally correspond to decoding performance with MVPA, this could partly reflect the ROI approach that was used. A whole-brain MVPA mapping approach might well reveal other regions that code action preparation that are not activated (or not selectively activated) in the univariate sense.

9) The authors note the increased sensitivity of their method relative to a univariate approach, but MVPA (like any other method) carries assumptions and limitations that should shape how the data are interpreted. This could be discussed.

10) The authors report MVPA analyses at each time point, yet we did not find much in the discussion of the results about how these decoding effects develop over time.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that tool use involves multiple distributed neural representations: effector-independent coding in posterior IPS and premotor cortex (where hand and tool action plans share representations), effector-specific coding in SPOC/EBA (hand-selective) and SMG/pMTG (tool-selective), and effector-specific coding in anterior parietal regions and motor cortex (both effectors decoded but no cross-decoding). This hierarchical organization suggests separate processing at lower levels with integration at higher frontoparietal levels.
results.result_reasoning: The claims are supported by converging MVPA decoding results showing distinct patterns across brain regions (C15-C19, C31-C34), with appropriate statistical tests (repeated-measures ANOVA with post-hoc comparisons, FDR correction). The experimental design using reverse tongs effectively dissociates kinematics from action goals (C22-C23), and control analyses in auditory cortex (C36-C37) and non-brain ROIs rule out confounds. The hierarchical interpretation (C6) follows logically from the spatial distribution of effector-specific vs effector-independent representations.

results.result: The experimental design used 13 right-handed subjects performing delayed reach-to-grasp or reach-to-touch movements with either hand or reverse tongs. The reverse tongs required opposite kinematics compared to hand use, allowing dissociation of action goals from motor kinematics. Time-resolved decoding showed predictive information arose in the two time points before movement, never before the auditory instruction, and was temporally separable from execution-related decoding.
results.result_reasoning: The methodological claims are well-documented with clear descriptions of sample size (C20), task design (C21-C23), and temporal characteristics of decoding (C28-C30). The use of reverse tongs is a critical design feature that effectively addresses the research question by maintaining constant action goals while varying kinematics. The time-resolved analyses provide strong evidence for planning-specific signals distinct from execution.

results.result: The authors demonstrate a coupling between visual category selectivity and motor planning: body-selective EBA decoded hand actions only, tool-selective pMTG decoded tool actions only, while tool-selective t-aIPS decoded both hand and tool actions. The decoding occurred during the planning phase, indicating these signals reflect motor intentions rather than sensory feedback. This suggests occipitotemporal cortex plays a role in action planning with effector-specific forward-state estimation.
results.result_reasoning: The claims are supported by independent localization of category-selective regions using a separate localizer experiment (C60, C62) followed by MVPA on motor task data. The temporal specificity of decoding during the planning phase (C66) provides strong evidence against sensory feedback explanations. However, the functional interpretation regarding forward-state estimation (C67) is somewhat speculative, though it is appropriately framed as a possibility rather than a definitive conclusion.

results.result: Control analyses in somatosensory cortex showed decoding only during movement execution (not planning), consistent with its sensory role. Motor cortex showed within-effector decoding but no across-effector decoding, consistent with its role in generating effector-specific muscle commands and hand kinematics.
results.result_reasoning: These control findings (C38-C39) provide important validation of the MVPA approach by showing expected null effects during planning in SS-cortex and expected effector-specific coding in motor cortex. The interpretations (C40) are well-grounded in established knowledge about motor cortex function (C46-C47) supported by appropriate citations. These results strengthen confidence in the positive findings in other regions.

results.result: Voxel weight analysis showed no consistent topography within or across subjects. Control analysis in auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus) showed across-effector decoding emerged earlier (fourth volume) than in frontoparietal cortex (fifth-sixth volumes), making it unlikely that frontoparietal effector-invariant responses are attributable to auditory cue commonalities.
results.result_reasoning: The voxel weight analysis (C35) appropriately acknowledges the lack of spatial structure, which is reasonable given the relatively low decoding accuracies (~55%) and known trial-to-trial variability in planning signals. The auditory cortex control (C36-C37) is a critical analysis that addresses a major alternative explanation, and the temporal dissociation provides strong evidence against the auditory confound interpretation.

results.result: The authors interpret that SPOC and EBA fail to incorporate tools into the body schema (based on lack of tool decoding), while SMG and pMTG play a selective role in generating tool actions. The anterior IPS is recruited for both hand and tool planning but uses different underlying representations (no cross-decoding), clarifying its role differs from previous interpretations suggesting shared representations.
results.result_reasoning: These interpretations follow logically from the decoding patterns: lack of tool decoding in hand-selective regions (C42) and lack of hand decoding in tool-selective regions (C45) support the body schema interpretation. The aIPS findings (C50-C51) appropriately revise previous interpretations by distinguishing between recruitment for both effectors versus shared representations, which is an important conceptual distinction supported by the cross-decoding results.

results.result: The authors speculate that effector-independent responses in posterior IPS may emerge from common coding of object features (contact points, orientation, mass distribution) that are relevant for grasping with both hand and tool, which could explain why classifiers trained on one effector can decode the other.
results.result_reasoning: This is explicitly presented as speculation (C53-C54) about the mechanism underlying across-effector decoding. While plausible and consistent with known pIPS functions, the study does not directly test whether object feature coding drives the cross-decoding. Additional experiments manipulating object features while holding actions constant would be needed to support this mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: The introduction and discussion contextualize the findings within established literature on tool use, body schema, mirror neurons, hierarchical motor control, occipitotemporal organization, and motor affordances. These claims provide theoretical framework and cite relevant prior work.
results.result_reasoning: These claims appropriately cite relevant literature and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide necessary context for interpreting the current findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made, though detailed verification of each cited work is beyond the scope of this review. The theoretical frameworks cited (hierarchical motor control, body schema, mirror neurons, motor affordances) are well-established in neuroscience.

results.result: The authors conclude that forward-state estimations in occipitotemporal cortex remain effector-specific, that the matching of visual selectivity and motor planning in EBA/pMTG is compatible with theories linking OTC organization to motor connectivity, and that visual categorical responses in OTC are linked to preparing related motor behaviors.
results.result_reasoning: These broader interpretive claims (C69, C73, C77) are well-supported by the empirical findings showing effector-specific decoding in occipitotemporal regions and the matching of visual category selectivity with motor decoding profiles. While these interpretations involve some inference beyond the direct data, they are appropriately qualified and represent reasonable conclusions from the pattern of results. The link to theoretical frameworks about OTC organization is appropriately presented as compatible rather than definitive.

results.result: The study found effector-specific decoding patterns in different brain regions: SPOC and EBA showed hand-specific decoding, while SMG and pMTG showed tool-specific decoding. These findings demonstrate that different regions selectively represent upcoming actions for specific effectors.

The reviewers accept these effector-specific decoding results without questioning their validity, only requesting better presentation.

This consistency across effectors could be responsible for some or even all of the apparently cross-effector classification.' This concern directly challenges whether the across-effector decoding reflects genuine goal-level representations or merely auditory cue content. The reviewers state 'This issue must be addressed.'

results.result: In anterior parietal regions (aIPS) and motor cortex, pre-movement activity patterns discriminated planned actions of both hand and tool but could not be used to predict actions across effectors, suggesting these regions code both effectors but with distinct underlying representations dependent on kinematics.

results.result: The study found a strong coupling between categorical visual selectivity and motor planning selectivity: body-selective EBA decoded hand action plans while tool-selective pMTG decoded tool action plans, with these signals reflecting motor intention rather than sensory feedback.
results.result_reasoning: Reviewer 4 explicitly endorses this interpretation, stating 'The authors' findings, showing that occipital temporal regions can decode upcoming actions would seem to resonate with that type of an explanation of the causes of neural specificity for different classes of visual stimuli in the ventral stream.' The reviewers accept this coupling as an important finding, though they encourage fuller discussion of its theoretical implications.

results.result: Time-resolved decoding analyses showed that predictive movement information arises in the two time points prior to movement initiation, never before the auditory instruction cue, and can be fully disentangled from movement execution signals that arise later.

results.result: Visual inspection of voxel weightings from the classifiers failed to reveal any structured or consistent topography within or across subjects.

results.result: Control analyses in Heschl's gyrus showed that accurate across-effector classification arises distinctly earlier in the planning phase compared to frontoparietal areas, suggesting the effector-invariant responses in frontoparietal cortex are not fully attributable to auditory commonalities in the planning cues.
results.result_reasoning: While this control analysis attempts to address the auditory confound concern, Reviewer 3 states 'It would be good to see the results (e.g., in figure form, and reduced statistics) for the control analysis of decoding of the ventricle and outside of the brain...it should be dealt with in full (rather than just saying the analysis was performed and there were no effects).' Reviewer 5's concern about auditory cues 'must be addressed' indicates the current control analyses are insufficient.

results.result: The overall finding that tool use is subserved by multiple distributed action-centered neural representations that are both shared with and distinct from those of the hand, with a hierarchical organization where hand and tool actions are represented separately at earlier levels before integration in frontoparietal cortex.
results.result_reasoning: The reviewing editor states 'The paper is clearly written and organized, and tackles an important question with a well-thought-out and sophisticated approach. Overall this is excellent work.' This indicates general acceptance of the main findings and hierarchical framework, though specific methodological concerns need addressing.

results.result: The findings suggest that occipitotemporal regions may play a role in action planning by predicting sensory consequences of movements in an effector-specific manner, and that the organization of occipitotemporal cortex may reflect connectivity patterns with motor structures rather than purely bottom-up visual properties.
